speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: FURTHER REPORT ON CONSTRUCTION AND ESTIMATED COST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,-1 wish to make a statement with reference to the Prime Minister's residence.
In the supplementary estimates to be tabled by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) the government is asking parliament to vote $300,000 for the completion of the Prime Minister's residence. This amount is in addition to $80,000 already included in the main estimates, and $30,000 expended in the fiscal year which ended on March 31 of this year, or a total of $410,000.
I admit at once that this figure, which includes $305,000 for the cost of the building and $105,000 for the furnishing of the house, is higher than the rough estimates of cost which were given to the government at the time the decision to provide an official residence for the Prime Minister was made in September of last year.
We were warned by the architects at that time that no satisfactory estimate could be made of the cost of reconstructing an old house until the work was far enough advanced 55946-256.1
to enable the architects to make a firm estimate of the soundness of the structure, and the extent to which it would have to be torn down and replaced by new construction.
As a result of their preliminary examination, the architects estimated that the cost of removing the old building and replacing it with a new modern building of similar proportions and dignity would be about $360,000. The architects considered that the existing structure could be rebuilt for a smaller amount, which is proving to be the fact, assuming that the preliminary estimate of cost of a new house is correct.
Rightly or wrongly, the government decided to rebuild the existing structure and, as I said on June 8, the government secured the services of an architectural firm which seemed to have the widest experience in this type of work, and of a local contractor with a first-class reputation.
Since the decision to rebuild was made, two factors have combined to increase considerably the estimated cost. In the first place, as the demolition of the interior of the house proceeded, it was found that the structure had deteriorated to an extent that the house practically had to be rebuilt, except for the outside walls and one or two main partitions. In the second place, building costs have risen substantially since last September.
It can be argued that the government should have decided to build a new residence, perhaps on a smaller scale than the existing house. However, the decision was made to rebuild the old residence. I gave the reasons for that decision in an earlier discussion on this subject.
As the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) pointed out at that time, once we had made substantial progress on the reconstruction of the present building, it was too late to change the decision, assuming that a change should have been made, which I do not admit. The problem then was to make the old building into a suitable modern residence. That is what is being done, and we are not spending a dollar which is not required to create an official residence for our Prime Minister which will be worthy of Canada.
When the house is completed it will not be a palace-I might just remind the hon. members by way of comparison that it is estimated the reconstruction of the White

Trans-Canada Highway House will cost $5,400,000-but it will be a dignified and well-equipped official residence where the Prime Minister can receive appropriately the representatives of any country, and in its beautiful setting, the residence will be an addition to the national capital of which the people of Canada can be proud.

speechtext:
Perhaps I should make a short statement. I think the purpose of this act is best described in the words of the original protocol between Canada and the United States-for the avoidance of double taxation and the prevention of fiscal evasion in the case of income tax. In a country such as Canada, which has close business interests with both the United Kingdom and the United States, it is very important that we avoid double taxation on the same income in order not to impede business between ourselves and the United States or between ourselves and Great Britain. It is also very important that our taxing authorities co-operate to see that there is no opportunity for evasion by taxpayers because of different taxation laws in the two countries.
It is not easy to negotiate such a tax convention, for several reasons. The most obvious one, of course, is the fact that the taxing laws of Canada and the United States are by no means identical. A second factor is the difference in legal terminology. A third factor, and a very important one, is that in such conventions the revenue loss through a concession must be roughly equal to the revenue we are going to gain through a similar concession from the other party. Because of the similarity between our tax laws and those of Britain, we have been able in the past to have our tax conventions with the United Kingdom more advanced than the ones we have with the United States. During recent years, however, continuous negotiation at Washington has resulted in this present Canada-United States taxing agreement coming much closer to the Canada-United Kingdom agreement. That, of course, is a good thing in the interests of business between all three countries.
The present amendments can be discussed in detail as we go through them, but the principal one in the first part, the income tax part, is to widen the present exemptions for workers of one country on temporary duty in the other country.

The second provision refers to succession duties. Under the old act the situs of stock left in estates was spelled out; the rest was left to the courts under the common law. Now we have a mutual arrangement spelling out in the act the situs of pretty well every class of property which might be left in an estate.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Thursday, June 22, consideration in committee of Bill No. 303, to amend the Canada Shipping Act, 1934- Mr. Chevrier-Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.
Sections 10 to 35 inclusive agreed to.
On section 36-Radio installation.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO RATIFY INTERNATIONAL CONVENTION FOR SAFETY OF LIFE AT SEA
speechtext:
Section 36 of this bill substitutes a new section 406, subsection 1, in the Canada Shipping Act, including a new paragraph (a) to which I wish to refer. The side-note reads "radio installation". This particular paragraph applies, of course, only to Canadian ships on international voyages. It does not apply to ships engaged in the coastal trade or on the great lakes. In accordance with the international convention for safety of life at sea, it makes certain provisions concerning radio installations which I believe are excellent. Members of the committee will observe that it provides that all Canadian ships carrying more than twelve passengers, and other Canadian ships of 1,600 gross tonnage-which of course refers only to cargo vessels-plying on an international voyage, must, unless they are exempted by the minister, be fitted with a radio installation which complies with the safety conventions. They must carry radio operators with such qualifications as are specified, who must keep such watches as the minister may prescribe, and in addition we find this provision: that while keeping watches the operator shall not engage in other duties which in any way interfere with the keeping of watches. That, of course, is taken from the international safety convention which applies to all ships of all maritime nations except Russia, which is not a party to the convention. It sets up a standard which I think is one which should be followed, not only for international voyages but also for certain of the ships on our coasts.
Under the Canada Shipping Act, subsection 2 of this section 406 deals with the domestic trade; in other words it contains the law applicable to the coastal trade. I should like the minister to correct me if I am wrong in any of these statements. Under subsection 2, paragraph (a), all passenger ships-this paragraph does not include cargo vessels-must have radiotelegraph installations provided that they are on voyages of a certain length. For example, if a ship is

licensed to carry from 50 to 250 passengers she must have radiotelegraph installation if she is going for more than 200 miles from one place to another place. Those are the words used in the act. If she is licensed to carry from 250 to 500 passengers, then she must have radiotelegraph installation if she is going for more than 90 miles from one place to another place. If she is a larger vessel licensed to carry over 500 passengers, then she must have this radiotelegraph installation with a radio operator if she is going for more than 20 miles from one place to another.
There is not the same provision in this subsection 2, which applies to the domestic trade, covering the watches that are to be kept. I should like to see it amended to contain the same provisions as are now to be applicable to all passenger ships on international voyages. In addition there is one great weakness in subsection 2 of section 406 of the act as it reads today, and that is the reference to the mileage which is described as being measured from one place to another place. The ordinary layman reading that section would think it meant that if a ship was going from Vancouver to Prince Rupert, which is a great deal more than 200 miles, it would have to have radiotelegraph installation and an operator. That is not the interpretation that has been placed on the section by some of the shipping companies. They say that "from one place to another place" means that if the ship stops every 200 miles in the case of a small ship, or every 90 miles in the case of a middle-sized ship, or every 20 miles in the case of a larger ship, then the provision does not apply and it is unnecessary to have radiotelegraph installation. That interpretation simply means that if these vessels call at a logging camp, a fish cannery, or any sort of whistle stop on the voyage up the west coast of Canada, they are not subject to this provision, and need not have radiotelegraph installation or an operator.
'My submission is that in effect they are evading the intent of the act. Because of the discovery of radiotelephony there is a distinct trend towards doing away with these radiotelegraph installations, or at least easing up on the provisions. Our dislike of this trend was clearly expressed in an editorial in one of the Vancouver papers two or three months ago, and I shall quote from the Vancouver Sun of March 13, 1950. The heading on the editorial is "Safety at Sea." Throughout my remarks I would stress that the whole issue here is safety at sea. We do not want to have a catastrophe on our coast by reason of one of the vessels plying up and down the coast not having the proper radiotelegraph
Canada Shipping Act
installation and an operator whose sole job is to look after it. I do not know whether I should quote this editorial, because it is praising a speech made by the hon. member for Skeena. However, it says:
Mr. Applewhaite urged that every ship of 50 or more tons and every ship chartered to carry passengers be required to carry at least one fulltime radio operator who shall have no other duties but the maintenance of radio equipment and keeping of radio watches. This demand may be extreme. The stress should be on the number of passengers carried and the distance of the voyage from point of origin to the most distant point.
You will notice that there they indicate that the words "from one place to another place" should not be used but "from the point of origin to the most distant point". The editorial continues:
The government should consider that ships carrying at least 50 persons including crew should be so protected. And it should also be remembered that the carrying of a full-time radio operator is not merely for the safety of the ship in question but to enable her to co-operate in rescuing other ships.
Maintenance of a full-time watch is also important. The operator should have no other duties that will interfere with his watch.
This question of interfering with the watch of the radio operator has arisen because some of the companies are trying to make the radio operators act also in other capacities- for example, as freight clerks or pursers or to have one of the officers do the job. They are trying to put other work on these men. That practice of course means that they are not available at all times to look after radiotelegraph on the ship. The editorial concludes:
There should be no distinction between international coastal voyages and domestic coastal voyages. A voyage from Vancouver to the Queen Charlottes can be just as dangerous as to Ketchikan.
A voyage from Vancouver to Seattle, or from Vancouver to Ketchikan, Alaska, or to Skagway, Alaska, is of course considered to be an international voyage. It therefore comes under subsection 1, which is being amended by the bill now before the committee. By the terms of this new subsection 1 there must be a radiotelegraph installation unless the minister exempts the ship, and there must be an operator keeping watches as set by the minister, and devoting his full time to the one business of looking after the radiotelegraph. A passenger on a trip from Vancouver to Seattle or from Vancouver to Alaska is thus protected. But a passenger on a voyage from Vancouver to Victoria or from Vancouver to Prince Rupert does not have that protection, although the voyage is just as dangerous. The ships have to go through the same difficult channels. They are exposed to the same open sea in certain places.

For example back in 1918 or 1919 the Princess Sophia was lost north of Prince Rupert and several hundred people were drowned. This whole question is one of safety of life at sea, as the Sun editorial points out.
We are deeply concerned about this matter. We believe that passengers on a coastal trip within Canada should have the same kind of protection that they get on a trip from a Canadian port to an American port. Certainly that one defect in the Canada Shipping Act should be removed-that is, the use of the phrase "from one place to another place." I ask that it be removed, because it is being misinterpreted by the shipping companies. Instead, I think those words should be "from the point of commencement to the farthest outward point", so that a ship carrying 50 to 250 passengers could go only 200 miles from the point of commencement to the farthest outward point without having a radiotelegrapher; a ship carrying from 250 to 500 passengers could go only 90 miles from the point of commencement to the farthest outward point, and a larger ship carrying 500 or more passengers could go only 20 miles from the point of commencement to the farthest outward point without carrying a radiotelegrapher.
It is quite possible that there might be some cases in which, by reason of the nature of the voyage, it is unnecessary to have a radiotelegrapher. In such a case the minister has power to grant an exemption. But the words I have suggested are the very words that the Department of Transport itself used in the fire regulations which were enacted on April 12 of this year. These fire regulations were put into effect as a result of the Noronic disaster and of the inquiry held by Mr. Justice Kellock. In paragraph 3 of the regulations hon. members will find this definition, under the head "Application": These regulations apply to all passenger steamships

I repeat that I am dealing only with passenger ships in requesting that a change be made in the act.
-registered in Canada employed in home-trade, inland or minor water voyages-
(a) which are certified to carry more than 25 berthed passengers or more than 50 berthed and unberthed passengers: or-
And this is the definition to which I refer particularly.
- (b) which do not carry berthed passengers but are certified to carry more than 100 unberthed passengers and the length of the voyage from the point of commencement to the farthest outward point exceeds fifteen miles or the distance from shore at any time exceeds five miles.
I am asking that subsection 2 of section 406 of the Canada Shipping Act be amended by substituting those words "from the point of commencement to the farthest outward point" for the words now found in that subsection, namely "from one place to another place". I should like to move:
That paragraph (a) of subsection 2 of section four hundred and six of the said act be amended by substituting for the words:
"from one plaae to another place" where they appear in clauses (i) (ii) and (iii) of the said paragraph, the following:
"from the point of commencement to the farthest outward point."
Frankly, Mr. Chairman, I probably should go further and ask for additional amendments to provide that the radiotelegraph operator must not be given other duties; but for the present I am moving this amendment in order to prevent the evasion of subsection 2 as it reads at the present time. I hope that the Minister of Transport will see fit to accept the amendment.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I take a few
moments to deal with the amendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra? I am sure he does not for one mpment take the position that the officers of the department are not seriously concerned about this section of the act dealing with the safety of life at sea along the coasts of Canada. I believe that was clearly established when section 406 and other sections were discussed in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.
Dealing with the amendment, however, I think there are general considerations to be examined. The first is the present position so far as section 406 is concerned. That position, as dealt with by section 406, covers the domestic trade-and by that I mean inland shipping, great lakes shipping and coastal shipping. Then there is the other aspect dealing with international shipping and international voyages as covered by the convention.
It has been the feeling of departmental officers all along that there should be a distinction between the requirements necessary

for international voyages and those in respect of inland or coastal voyages. That position has always been taken, and is recognized generally in the Canada Shipping Act. It was taken with reference to the steamship inspection regulations to which my hon. friend referred a moment ago.
While I am on that point may I say that while the hon. member in his amendment uses the language of the steamship inspection regulations, there are many members on his side of the house who thought those regulations were much too stringent. Indeed, what we attempted to do when we enacted the steamship regulations was to take a middle course between international and inland requirements in order to protect ships of that kind.
Leaving that position for the moment, let me say that the coasts of Canada-and I am referring particularly to the west coast-are pretty well protected by radio aids. It was clearly explained in committee that there is a difference between the range and effect of radiotelegraphy and radiotelephony. An expert from the department in radio matters indicated that radiotelegraphy should be considered on long voyages, international voyages, and that in so far as they were concerned it was more effective than radiotelephony. He did think however that a distinction should be made in respect to great lakes shipping, inland shipping and coastal shipping. He was of the opinion that the radiotelephone was effective, provided that there was a sufficient range, for coastal operations; and he thought that that condition obtained in connection with the west coast.
Then there is the general view among technical men-and of course I am not familiar with it, but only state what they say- that great developments are expected in the field of radiotelephony.

DEPARTMENT OF RESOURCES AND DEVELOPMENT National film board-
401. Administration, production and distribution of films, and other visual materials, including authority to finance temporary work performed for other public authorities or other agencies as the public interest requires, $2,092,413.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Resources and Development):
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO RATIFY INTERNATIONAL CONVENTION FOR SAFETY OF LIFE AT SEA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in view of the events which have taken place over the last six months affecting the administration of the national film board, it might be helpful to hon. members if I made a brief statement in introducing the estimates for the current year.
It will be remembered that on December 7 last I informed the house that the business administration of the film board was being examined by Messrs. J. D. Woods and Gordon Limited, a firm of business consultants. The committee will also remember that following a meeting of the board on December 15 a new film commissioner, Mr. W. A. Irwin, was appointed, effective February 1, 1950. These two moves, the survey undertaken by J. D. Woods and Gordon Limited, and the appointment of the new commissioner, have afforded an opportunity of assessing the value of the board's work, of taking steps to correct weaknesses which have appeared, and to some extent of charting the path of the board's future development.
It is fortunate also that the government, in considering the future of the board, should have the advantage of the advice of the royal commission on national development in the arts, letters and sciences, under the distinguished chairmanship of Right Hon. Vincent Massey, which has in recent months heard briefs presented by groups and organizations of all kinds in public hearings conducted in the principal cities across Canada.
On March 29 I tabled a copy of the report submitted by J. D. Woods and Gordon Limited. Hon. members have since had an opportunity to study the report and the recommendations it contains. It is not my intention to discuss in detail all the recommendations contained in the report, but I should like to make these observations.
The recommendations put forward in the J. D. Woods and Gordon Limited report fall into two main classifications:
1.	Recommendations requiring legislative authority before they can be implemented.
2.	Recommendations which could be implemented without legislative action.
Supply-Resources and Development
None of the recommendations in the first category has been implemented to date, although a bill is now ready for consideration by the house. I am able to report, however, that progress has been made in implementing some of the recommendations in the second category. An announcement has already been made by the film commissioner concerning the appointment of three senior personnel of the board-director of production, director of technical operations, and director of distribution.
The board has taken over its own internal accounting. The number of individual accounts has been reduced from more than
5,000	to about 1,000, and a system of accounting on an accrual rather than a cash basis has been established. I would point out, however, that the treasury branch of the Department of Finance will continue to operate a cash account for the board to pay out and receive moneys on a cash basis.
One of the recommendations of the report was that the film commissioner should review every activity in which the board is engaged to see whether any of them should be curtailed or transferred to other government departments or agencies. In the course of the past four months the commissioner has had an opportunity of surveying the various divisions of the board. It is too early yet, in view of other reorganization suggestions put forward by the report, to say which, if any, activities can be transferred or curtailed. However, this question is being pursued, and in due course I believe some action can be taken with respect to this recommendation.
After reviewing the report submitted by J. D. Woods and Gordon Limited, I am sure that hon. members will agree that many of its recommendations are sound and reasonable. The report does not recommend status as a crown corporation for the board, but it does indicate that it should be possible to establish the board within the regular governmental organization plan, at the same time providing the flexibility which is felt essential for its efficient operation.
In general I can therefore inform the committee that many of the recommendations contained in the Woods-Gordon report which do not require legislative action are already being implemented with a view-to improving the efficiency of the board's operations. At the same time careful consideration has been given to those recommendations requiring legislative action, and hon. members will shortly have an opportunity of considering a bill which is a complete revision of the National Film Act of 1939.

Supply-Resources and Development
Shortly after taking up his new duties, the film commissioner asked for and received from the board permission to have a survey of the board's technical services and equipment undertaken by a qualified expert. As a result the services of a highly qualified technician, formerly connected with the J. Arthur Rank Organization, were engaged for this purpose. His observations have been most helpful and will guide the board in its future technical development.
1 should like to say a word about security. On March 29 last I reported to the house that the screening of all employees of the board had been completed. At that time I said that three employees out of some 580 had been relieved of their duties for reasons connected with the screening. I have nothing further to report in this connection. The board is now a secure agency and is in a position to undertake work of a secret nature on behalf of all government departments.
During 1949-50 the efficiency of the board improved, with the result that greater production was achieved in all departments without increasing staff. Films were produced on a wide variety of subjects, including Newfoundland's entry into confederation, national parks, tourists, health, welfare and nutrition, resources and national development. One of the more outstanding productions of the year was an extraordinary film, "Challenge: Science against Cancer", which was made with the co-operation of the Department of National Health and Welfare and the National Cancer Institute of the United States Public Health Service.
Hon. members will be pleased to recall that the national film board again won an impressive number of awards for its films in competitions conducted in Canada and in other countries. The board received six awards in the Canadian film awards which are given with the participation of the Canadian Association for Adult Education. Awards were received from three film festivals in Italy, and others held in Brussels, Belgium, and Cleveland, Ohio. Two of the board's productions were included in a selection of the ten best 16 millimetre films of 1949 conducted by the American Scholastic Teachers' Magazine, New York city. The national committee on films for safety in the United States selected as the outstanding non-theatrical film in the occupational safety field the film "Safe Clothing", produced by the board for the Department of Labour.
The Woods-Gordon report comments favourably on the value of having a central body like the national film board to handle government photographic assignments. The

report points out that the board, by getting government departments to pool their still picture requirements, has produced for those departments many useful photographs at reasonable cost. Demand for the board's films for use on television is growing in the United States and the United Kingdom. Of particular interest to television stations in the United States are the board's films on travel which are produced for the Canadian government travel bureau.
In presenting the estimates of the national film board for 1950-51, it will be noted that this year the total figure submitted is $2,211,017, which represents an increase of $153,607 from 1949-50. It will also be noted that this year only two votes are submitted as against four votes last year. This is in conformity with the Woods-Gordon report, which recommended one vote for operations and another for purchase of equipment. Members will find on page 260 of the estimates the details of services under various headings of administration, production of films, distribution, and so on. The increase to which I have referred is occasioned largely by a rise in administration costs due to increased salaries. An additional $50,000 has been provided for production of films. An increase of $33,319 has been provided for distribution of films to permit the supply of more prints to rural and urban areas, and replacement of existing prints both in Canada and abroad.
In conclusion I should like to say that in my opinion the national film board has made a successful passage through a very difficult period. It is a tribute to the high morale of the staff that the board has maintained and even increased both production and distribution during the year. The work of the new commissioner has already been reflected in the work of the board. The deputy chairman, together with the six others who sit with him on the board, have given freely of their time and effort and have made a really worthwhile contribution. Last December I expressed the hope that the film board would come to be regarded everywhere without prejudice as an important instrument in the expanding life of Canada. I feel that since that time the board has taken firm steps in. that direction.

A message from His Excellency the Governor General, transmitting supplementary estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1951, was presented by Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance), read by Mr. Speaker to the house, and referred to the committee of supply.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Dion in the chair.
DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE General administration-
85. Departmental administration, $1,392,488.

Mr. Chairman, it seems appropriate that on the general administration item for the Department of Finance certain remarks should be made in connection with a subject which has been under discussion here on different occasions during the present session.
The public accounts committee has had a number of meetings, and is still sitting, but an interim report was tabled which dealt with certain recommendations made by that committee and certain evidence received by it. First of all I wish to make it clear that the interim report is not unanimous, and that while there are a number of recommendations in it which are useful and will be helpful to members of the House of Commons, and I would hope particularly useful to the Minister of Finance in the preparation of estimates for next year, the fact remains that there were certain im-
Supply-Finance
portant points put forward in the report which do not represent the views of some members of the committee.
The sittings of the committee have been useful in that, in addition to the discussion of the details of the public accounts, we had the advantage of recommendations by the Auditor General in regard to a great number of procedural matters which do suggest that important improvements can be made. One of the things emerging most clearly from the recommendations of the Auditor General was the emphasis on the fact that public accounts should be before members of the house, and estimates as well, in a form that would make it possible for hon. members to exercise supervision over public expenditures.
The recommendations were based quite clearly upon a recognition of the fact that the estimates and the public accounts as they come before the House of Commons and the examination and discussion of them in the house do not give to hon. members effective control over public expenditures unless they are so presented that hon. members are able to understand how the details are made up and to obtain the kind of information they should have.
One of the recommendations of the Auditor General was that the system of presenting the estimates and the public accounts should be simplified and information given in such a way that related subjects could be discussed with a knowledge of the facts behind the figures. One statement was prepared and placed in evidence before the committee which indicated the difficulty there is in dealing with the estimates in the way we now do.
An official of the Department of Finance prepared an analysis of the estimates now before us and of those for two other years, one of which was the last full year before the war. The information was broken down on what was described as a functional basis. It brought together related activities, and then accumulated the totals from each department.
What was apparent when those figures were brought together was the very large increase in a number of items out of all proportion to the increase in population of the country, or what would appear to be the normal business of government. Without attempting to review the whole of the statement, I should like to take a single item to show the extent to which expenditures have increased. Similar increases are found in many respects on almost the same proportionate basis as the one I shall now mention.

Supply-Finance
Under the heading of telephones, telegrams and postage, the total in 1938-39 was $960,248, whereas in the present estimates the total is $8,595,943. I shall not go into details of the other items, because similar increases, some on a larger and some on a smaller proportionate basis, occur right through this statement. I take that particular item to show how impossible it is from the practical point of view to examine the estimates here with any suggestion that we are actually performing an effective audit of the items and are in position to make specific recommendations in regard to reductions under one heading or another.
The total in regard to telephones, telegrams and postage is the combined total of the items in the estimates of different departments. We see a figure in front of us which requires explanation, but when dealing with each of these items separately it is impossible to say exactly what can be donq in the way of reduction consistent with efficiency. It was for that very reason that we proposed an examination of the whole system of accounting and the organization of government by an independent body. That proposal has been disposed of by a majority vote of this house for the present session, but it will be renewed again in the hope that in the meantime the government will have seen the advantage of such a method.
But even if that course were not adopted, there is another course which I submit should be adopted. This is the time to put this forward because when the estimates are being prepared next year they will be prepared before we have an opportunity to express our views on the subject. If the estimates were submitted to a committee on estimates we would have the nearest approach that we could have within our parliamentary structure to that type of independent examination formally put forward by motion in this house. A committee on estimates could deal with the estimates of each department by bringing the officials of the department before it. They could bring the items together, examine them and see exactly how they are made up and find out if there were any substantial economies which could be effected to the advantage of the public service and to the very great advantage of the taxpayers of Canada. If we did that we would only be doing what every large business is doing year by year, seeking to find out ways in which business can be carried on more efficiently and at reduced costs through the elimination of duplication of services and through a careful examination of how expenditures are actually incurred and how they are made up.

Without any suggestion as to the improper-use of these services under such headings as telephones, telegrams and postage, it is easy for everyone in this committee to understand how these things can get out of hand unless there is some effective measure of control. I do not believe that the Minister of Finance or his officials are better able to examine details of this kind in the very largest business in the country, the business of government, than are the experts in other types of business. They seek the examination by people who can examine from an objective point of view outside the actual organization itself.
We could examine details like this. We could examine details like travelling and transportation expenses which have grown from $4,742,206 in the last year before the war to $22,744,344 for the coming year. The Minister of Finance has said, "Point to single items where reductions could be made." That sounds like a practical suggestion, but except for the purposes of making a statement in this house every hon. member knows that it is not a practical suggestion. Every hon. member knows that the only way that members can obtain information which will make it possible to deal with this upon the basis of single items is to have a committee on estimates and also concurrently in the wider field an investigation such as we proposed in the resolution to which I have referred.
There has been a tendency during the present session when proposals were made for the appointment of committees of this kind to suggest that we are seeking to establish the system of government that is in operation in the United States and to depart from the practices described as British parliamentary institutions. Here is a case where that argument can have no validity because there is a committee on estimates at Westminster which has authority to call, and does call before it, senior officials and others who are in position to explain details and show exactly how the items are made up. On that basis that committee on estimates is able to make recommendations in detailed form.
What we are proposing is the adoption of a system which has worked satisfactorily for many years in a parliament which is described, outside the commonwealth as well as inside, as the mother of parliaments. Far from proposing any. departure from traditional parliamentary practices, we are merely proposing that we adopt parliamentary practices which have been carried on successfully in that parliament from which we drew our general practices and traditions.
To sum up the items under the various headings, we arrive at a total showing that

the estimates for the last year before the war required a total of $549,219,048, while this year the estimates call for $2,367,480,478. When we suggest that economies can be effected the answer is given, as it was given just a few days ago, that a substantial part of the estimates of most of the departments is made up of items for services of a statutory nature which cannot be reduced. When that explanation is given it invariably overlooks the fact that wrapped in those total costs is the cost of handling services and that an independent examination might well disclose large numbers of items where reductions could be made in the handling of the services, to the advantage of the government and to the advantage of the taxpayers of Canada.
The proposals made by the Auditor General were not accepted in the report presented by the public accounts committee. I am not suggesting for a moment that the recommendations of the Auditor General should be accepted without question. I can see real arguments against reducing the number of items, as was suggested. I can see no arguments against simplification of the presentation of the accounts and the giving of greater detail in that part of the statement of estimates explaining the items found in the front part of the book.
Moreover, I have heard no sound argument put forward suggesting any reason why a committee on estimates would not be the best procedure for t^ie year by year examination of the estimates. I do not think any argument was put forward before the committee suggesting any reason for not making the recommendation that there should be a committee on estimates to deal with estimates presented to the house in future. I also think the recommendation which was made with respect to explanation of details and steps being taken to give parliament effective, practical and real control over expenditures is one which should be emphasized and carried into effect.
I am making these comments now because the Minister of Finance is the minister primarily charged with the responsibility for the preparation of the estimates and the form in which we shall receive them. There is a lack of uniformity in the way in which they are presented. While the reduction of the number of items in some departments may be questioned, there certainly can be no such question in the case of the Department of National Defence where the bulk of the expenditure on national defence is included in a single item. Furthermore, the supporting details given at the back of the book do not explain these enormous expenditures, today approaching the total of the budgets of the government before the war, in a way
Supply-Finance
that makes it possible for members to make any real examination of these estimates. If there is a single department which demonstrates the necessity for following a number of the recommendations of the Auditor General it is the Department of National Defence.
As I pointed out in discussion of its estimates earlier, it does not follow the same procedure as other departments in regard to the construction of buildings and other things of that kind, which cannot by any possible stretch of the imagination be regarded as secret. I urge the Minister of Finance to give careful consideration to the recommendations of the Auditor General. I hope that after consideration thereof he will arrange for the presentation of the estimates next year in a form which will be more understandable to members and which will follow some uniform pattern in each department so far as that is practicable. I hope he will also inform the house that he is going to agree to the setting up of a committee on estimates shortly after the opening of the next session.
All hon. members know that during the time we have sat here this argument has been before the other place and has also been discussed in public. Hon. members are also aware that not only in Canada but also in other nations of the commonwealth and in the United States there is constant emphasis on the fact that the greatest need today in the field of government activity is to find a way of exercising effective control over expenditure so that, with the enormous expenditures made by many agencies not subject to the ordinary supervision of parliament or even of government, the highest measure of accounting efficiency may be established and the most economical practices adopted. Many of those who have put forward these contentions have emphasized the fact that our whole democratic structure may break down unless we are able to exercise control of the amount of expenditure by so many agencies of the government as well as by the government itself.
For the very reasons that have been given it is not possible to deal with single items here. The public accounts committee deals with past accounts; a committee on estimates could deal with the present estimates before us and other estimates in the years ahead. The most that we can do now is to say that the system that has been adopted is one which denies that measure of detail which would make it possible to recommend reductions, except in a few simple cases. We must therefore urge a procedure which has worked well elsewhere, and would work equally well

Supply-Finance
here, so that in the future we may be able to consider the estimates with actual knowledge of the facts.
The question before the Minister of Finance and other members of the house is whether the machinery set up by parliament is to be machinery which will really carry on the business of parliament and the government in the most efficient way, or whether it is to be machinery which will be used for the purpose of hiding information. Those who have sat as members of some of the committees this year know very well that there are numerous instances of steps being taken to use the machinery now available for the purpose of hiding information instead of exposing it to the examination of members of the house. What we do should be for the purpose of reducing costs wherever costs can be reduced, for the purpose of increasing in every way the efficiency of the biggest business in Canada, for which members of the house are primarily responsible, and urging the taking of steps for next year which will make it possible for us to deal effectively with the estimates that come before us at that time.

I want to
raise one question with the minister which is really a matter of finance. When we were discussing the public works estimates the other night the question of commitments arose. I hope the minister is aware that it was then suggested, and I hope agreed, that the whole question of commitments might be dealt with in more detail on the estimates of the Department of Finance. I should like to know whether it would be more convenient to discuss the matter now or later.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It might be as convenient to
take it up now as any other time. The position with respect to commitments is this. As my hon. friend and the committee are aware, under British constitutional practice there is no limit to the commitments a government may make under contracts which will carry on in future years. The making of those commitments or the giving of those undertakings does, of course, imply that parliament will have to vote the necessary funds in succeeding years, and that in making such commitments the government of the day must feel that it is going to be in a position to implement them.
The practice with respect to commitments in the past has been varied, but my understanding is that where a specific amount has been voted, say in the estimates of the Department of Public Works, encumbrances would not be issued beyond the total of the amount voted. There was nothing to prevent commitments being entered into which would fall due in future years. The practice we

have followed the last year or two of inserting specific commitment authority in a particular vote is for the purpose of limiting the extent of the commitments that may be made by that particular department for the particular purposes indicated. In the absence of such specific statutory limitation on commitments, the department of course would be perfectly free to make any commitment it saw fit. As I have indicated, the purpose of inserting a specific amount as commitment authority was to limit the department in the commitments it might incur. Does that cover the point my hon. friend had in mind?

Yes and no.
When we were considering the estimates of the Department of Public Works the other evening it became clear that there was a whole list of substantial commitments. We asked the minister to let us know to what extent those had been availed of, and my recollection is that the extent was comparatively trivial. So the question arose as to whether there was any need for these substantial amounts, running into many hundreds of thousands of dollars earmarked against various items, or whether it might not be more sensible to have a common fund.
I digress for a moment. I am a little surprised-perhaps I took it up wrongly- to hear the minister say there is nothing to prevent a department making commitments of any size; that is, I suppose nothing except common sense. Does the minister mean that literally?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is quite right. There is no constitutional limitation on the minister of a department, with the approval of the government, entering into contracts for any amount he sees fit.

I suppose I understand the sense in which the minister makes that statement. It would not mean a thing except the hope that later on parliament would grant those amounts. I find it a little difficult to understand the minister's explanation that this really is not an enabling provision but a limiting provision.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is exactly what it is, and what it is intended to be.

It seemed to me he regarded it as merely some additional leeway given to his department if it should find itself pinched here and there. Let me put a specific question. The practice now in connection with public works expenditures, as the committee is aware, is to indicate in the details the estimated cost of the various public projects by provinces. A lump sum is voted, which represents the best estimate the department can give as to the amount of money that actually will be expended on all those projects in the particular fiscal period. In their experience it has been found that if they were to list one hundred different projects such as wharves, breakwaters, public buildings and so on, some can proceed more rapidly than others, and if they are restricted to each individual vote there is a substantial overestimate of what will be the probable expenditure. In addition to that, in the public works estimates there is specific authority to incur commitments for future years; but, as I have said before, that is intended as a limitation so the department will not place contracts now extending into future years beyond the amount indicated in the particular item.

Will the minister make a statement on the apparent shortage of venture capital in Canada? The other day I referred to a statement made by the deputy governor of the Bank of Canada, in which he stated that thrifty Canadians had increased their savings by $3 billion in the past four years, and were increasing their savings at the rate of $400 million a year. These savings were adequate to meet the investment needs of Canada, but apparently Canadians were not prepared to take the risk. Consequently the United States investor is stepping in to put money into the resources of this country.

The situation has now developed where 50 per cent of the dividends of all corporations in Canada are being paid to non-residents. Is the minister considering taking any steps to encourage people to invest their money in the resources of Canada?
I suggested that it might help the situation if the government were to refund part of the maturing dominion bonds through the Bank of Canada. This would increase the amount of investment capital and would als'o help in reducing the national debt, and consequently the rates of tax; that in itself would help encourage investing. It seems as though the financial institutions of this country are far more interested in investing money in bonds than in investing money in the resources of the country. We hear members deplore the fact that we have adopted a form of paternalism towards the people of this country, but it does seem to me that we have done that to a far greater extent towards our financial institutions. They apparently require a government guarantee against loss before they are prepared to make an investment in such things as farm improvement loans, housing, or business loans for veterans. Surely our own financial institutions should be prepared to show a more venturesome spirit. If it were not quite so easy for them to invest their capital in bonds, then they might be prepared to enter the legitimate field of developing the resources of this country. If the United States investors are prepared to do it, there is no reason why the Canadians should not be prepared to do it.
I suggested also that it might be. worth giving consideration to setting up the securities commission, or an investment advisory board, on a voluntary basis. Then companies desiring to obtain capital could apply to this board, pay a licence fee, and a statement of their circumstances would be published. It would help to give the people who are desirous of investing money a better understanding of the proposition being placed before them. Has the minister given any consideration to that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, I listened with a great deal of interest the other day to the useful speech that was made by my hon. friend from Acadia. I am just as interested as he is in encouraging venture capital. I think that capital should be perhaps more venturesome than it is. So far as the government is concerned, we have taken some measures to encourage it to be so; the ten per cent tax credit on dividends, the reduction of the income tax on small business corporations and the liberalization of investment powers of 55946-257
Supply-Finance
insurance companies and trust and loan companies, which passed this house a few days ago, and so on.
As every member of this house knows, we have been in the midst of a capital investment boom in this country over the last three or four years. Actually the proportion of our national income that is going into capital expenditures today is higher than ever before in the history of Canada, and I am told higher in proportion than any other country in the world. I think that is a satisfactory situation, and I am glad to see it happen. I think most of it is going into enterprises which will make for greater prosperity. I do not think it is entirely fair to say that either Canadian individuals or Canadian financial institutions are lacking in a venturesome sprit or a desire to invest in Canadian enterprise.

I should like to draw to the attention of the minister a statement he made not very long ago, that if the committee wanted information it was their duty and the duty of the opposition to ask as many questions as possible to secure that information. That was a proper thing for the Minister of Finance to say, and I hope this committee will take advantage of it today.
There is one item in particular which I brought up at every session. I want to compliment the minister for giving us that information in a more comprehensive way. I refer to the amounts we are asked to vote, namely, $8,774,178, or almost one-third of the total amount of money voted, and for which we have no details, except that we can find out how many temporary employees there are. According to the record that I have here in the detail, there are 4,318 temporary employees, and these receive the average salary of a little over $2,000 per year. I think it would be quite in order for the department to put in a list, the same as they do with the regular civil servants, showing how many of these were economists, how many were supervisors and so on all through the various categories, showing what they are working at and what are their salaries.
We have not any account of that whatsoever. When a little over 30 per cent of the total vote is there as a blank cheque, I think that we should get some information about this matter. I raise the matter again because, as I said, in the last four or five years we have gained this much. We now know how many temporary employees there are. We

87.	Superannuation and retirement acts, administration, $188,700.

I just want to speak for a
few minutes on this item, although I had intended to speak for forty minutes. The parliamentary assistant has been over here and he has sort of worn me down.

He is not
going away too, is he?

I want to refer to a small
group of people in this country who suffer a certain hardship and injustice by the present superannuation act and the regulations. I have run into an occasional case here and there, and I am just bringing this matter to the attention of the minister to see whether something can be done to amend the regulations or order in council or anything of that sort, just in order to take in a small number of people, as far as I can see, who are affected in various departments of government.
I am just going to mention one case in order to illustrate the situation. In the city of Nelson we have a young man who has been twenty years in the employ of the post office. He was eight years in the employ of the postmaster before the post office was made a revenue post office. Then it was made a revenue post office and he became a civil servant; and he has been twelve years a civil servant. When he became a civil servant he was allowed to come under the superannuation act, I understand, as were the postmasters. But at that time neither postmasters nor clerks were permitted to pay up back superannuation for the years they had previously been employed. But since that time, owing to the order in council that was passed on December 24, 1948, I understand the postmaster has been permitted to pay up his superannuation for all the years he has served the government, even including the time prior to his actually being a civil servant. There are in that post office a few men who paid superannuation since but who are not permitted to pay their back superannuation as the postmaster did. One of these young men has contracted an incurable disease. He has been in hospital for six months and cannot possibly live but a short time longer. He is actually dying at the present time and because of the provisions of the superannuation act, his wife is left with that limited amount of security.
I want to ask the minister if he thinks it is possible for this matter to be given consideration, not only for the sake of this unfortunate civil servant but for that of a small number of others also who are willing to pay up their superannuation in order to provide their wives with a satisfactory security. The sad part of this case also is that this young man's sick leave allowance has now also been discontinued by the post office, so that he and his wife are absolutely flat after his having worked for this country as a civil servant for twenty years. I should like the minister to make a study of the situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I shall be glad to do that. My hon. friend and I have had a little bit

of correspondence, I think, about the case to which he has referred.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: With the pressure of other matters, I do not know that I have answered his last letter, but I have been looking at it. As he, of course, realizes, the difficulty is this. Employees of revenue postmasters were at no time government employees. I know the situation because my grandfather and my uncle after him were revenue postmasters for a great many years. The system there is that the postmaster gets commission on his stamp sales, his money orders, box rentals and so on, and he hires and pays his own staff. That is the traditional position of the revenue postmaster. His employees are not, during the term of employment, government employees and never were. He of course at all times has been a government employee. That is the distinction between the postmaster and the people whom he hires. But I shall be glad to study the situation to which my hon. friend refers and to see whether anything can be done.
Thank you.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I hope the minister, despite the heat and the time of the session, is ready to discuss in some detail the question as to providing a cost of living bonus or some other supplementation for superannuated civil servants, especially for those whose pensions are in the lower brackets. It certainly is not necessary for me to speak at length on this matter, because I have spoken on it a good many times. I am sure the minister must be prepared. He must have known that when this item was called I would have something to say about it. Fortunately I came into the chamber just in time for this item. We have just concluded another meeting of our committee on old age security, and I came directly here, although I did not know that we were going to reach this item quite so soon.
As the minister knows from figures that have been placed on Hansard, there are quite a number of retired employees of this government whose pensions are a disgrace. I am looking at the answers to questions of mine as recorded at page 834 of Hansard of March 16, 1950. I find that, as at February 28, 1950, there were 253 retired civil servants on pensions of less than $20 per month.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Some probably with extremely short service.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
And they will live a very short time on that sort of pension, too. There were 498 whose pensions were $20 or over but less than $30 a month. There

were 677 whose pensions were $30 of over but less than $40 a month, and so on. All told there are 4,584 retired civil servants whose pensions are less than $80 a month. The table at page 834 gives more details on that, but I have picked the $80 figure because it is the old age pension figure for a man and wife, both on pension, at the present time.
As I have said there are 4,584 retired civil servants of the federal government whose pensions are less than that amount. In addition there are 871 widows of retired civil servants whose pensions are less than $20 a month, and there is a total of 2,516 widows of retired civil servants whose pensions are less than $40 a month. I take that $40 figure for widows because that is the old age pension for a widow, by herself.
The minister knows this whole problem has been brought to his attention a good many times. Indeed, it was first brought to the attention of the Department of Finance when Mr. Ilsley held the finance portfolio, which means that it has been on the desk of the present Minister of Finance ever since he took over the department. He gave it a fair amount of consideration early in the game, but that seemed to end with the issuing of a statement which indicated that the government felt it should not do something which was not being done generally by others who paid pensions to retired employees. I have pointed out on other occasions that at least three governments I know of are paying supplementary amounts to their retired civil servants. The three I have mentioned are the governments in the United Kingdom, the province of Newfoundland and the province of Saskatchewan. There may be others of which I am not aware; but at least these three do something for their superannuated civil servants, especially those in the lower brackets.
The plan of supplementing civil servants'' pensions so far as the United Kingdom is concerned began back during the war years when the coalition government was in power, and has been continued and in fact amended upwards since the Labour government took office. So there are at least three governments that recognize that, despite the contractual nature of civil service pensions, they have a responsibility toward their former employees.
I might point out that, small though it is, the Canadian Pacific Railway makes a small addition to the pensions of their employees who are in very low brackets. That supplementation applies only between the time an employee goes on pension and the time he qualifies for old age pension. It is not all it could be, but at least it is a gesture on

Supply-Finance
the part of that railway company. My colleague from Kootenay West tells me that Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company does the same thing.
Even if there were not any examples of other employers doing this sort of thing, it seems to me there is a moral responsibility resting upon the government to give a lead to other employers. However, there are these examples and I think that, rather than lag behind provincial governments such as Newfoundland and Saskatchewan, where their resources are limited, this federal government should be taking the lead in an important matter of this kind.
As the minister knows, and as I am sure hon. members in all parts of the house know, this is something of such concern to the people affected that they have organized themselves into associations in various parts of the country. There is a very active branch of their association in Quebec city, as well as in Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg, Vancouver, Victoria, and a group of them here in Ottawa. These associations and their various branches have made their representations from time to time 'to the government. They have also been in touch with their various members of parliament, particularly those members from the areas where these associations are organized.
In other words members of parliament generally, from the correspondence they have received and the representations made to them, must know just how serious is the plight of these people and how strongly they feel that they have a moral claim upon the government, their former employer, to do something about the situation. They have been assured many times by various members of the house that consideration would be given to their plight. I remember on one occasion making the statement that particularly during the last election compaign, many Liberal candidates in British Columbia assured their constituents that they would go to bat on this question. At that particular point the hon. member for Coast-Capilano interjected something to the effect that he had not made any such promises. As he knows, he has since received a letter from one of the associations at the coast reminding him of the promise he made to them in a letter concerning this matter. I know he has received such a letter because the same association wrote to me a letter with which they enclosed a copy of the letter sent to him. I have not that letter with me because, as I have said, I have just come from the committee on old age security and have not had time to go to my office to get my file. However, I just wish to make the point that hon. members

generally, and particularly at election times, in those centres where these people are concentrated, have felt that their plight has been sufficient for those hon. members to give varying grades of assurance that they would go to bat for those people in parliament, or by making representations to the government. I feel that the case has been brought forcefully to the attention of the government, and that it has been done repeatedly. In the past delegations have appeared before the minister, and it does seem to me that on moral grounds in this year of 1950 there simply is no excuse for an employer as well off as the federal government to be paying to any of its former employees pensions as low as $20 or $30 a month, and these various other figures I have mentioned.
I am familiar with the argument about the contractual basis of these pensions, but I suggest that that argument disappears when one realizes what has happened. The value of the dollar and the whole question of our economic situation is at least to some extent under the control of the federal government. These people feel that they are getting back now-from the fund into which they put their contributions-dollars which are by no means worth what the dollars were worth that they put into that fund, and they contend that the argument by the government about the contractual aspect of the matter does not hold at all.
I need not extend the argument. The case has been well put forward by these people in their letters to the government and to members of parliament. The case has been well put forward by representatives of these branches who have come to Ottawa and have waited upon members of parliament. I am sure many hon. members who are listening to me now will recall that those representations have been made to them both by letter and in person. I trust that other hon. members in all sections of the house will support me in this plea to the minister to give favourable consideration to the request that something be done to supplement the pensions of these retired civil servants, particularly in the case of those persons whose pensions are in the lower brackets.

If the minister is not going to reply I would draw his attention to one phase of the situation in Newfoundland. When people have been pensioned by the provincial government they receive a cost of living bonus because the cost of living is 80 per cent above what it was in 1939.
As one who had something to do with getting that, as president of the civil service association for 15 years, I know how people

feel when they do not get it. I had a case drawn to my attention of a postmistress who was pensioned and who had to wait six months before she got her pension. When she got it she found that she was not getting the cost of living bonus. Is the minister in a position to tell us anything about that matter? It has been brought to his attention before.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend will recall that service in Newfoundland is added to service of the civil servant for Canada, and the appropriate pension is paid. The provincial government of Newfoundland in effect pays the portion of the pension attributable to the Newfoundland service and the federal government pays the difference. I do not think that special rates could be made with respect to pensions payable in Newfoundland. The terms on which the pensions are payable were fixed by the terms of union and confirmed by the statute. I would not think it would be feasible to have one level of pensions in one province of Canada and another level in the other provinces.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: But it would be feasible to make arrangements, by an item in the estimates, or better still by legislation, to provide a scale of supplementation across the country *which would make possible a greater percentage of increase for those in the lower brackets. I hope the minister will not try to get this item through without discussing it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not want to get it through without discussing it and I shall be glad to discuss it. I think I can discuss it very shortly by saying that the government's position has not changed from that indicated in the statement I made last year. I know my hon. friend is intensely interested in this question. Among his other attractive qualities he has the capacity of repeating at intervals practically the same speech-I do not blame him-perhaps in the hope that the government will change its mind. But there would be no purpose in repeating my speech of last year on this matter because in substance it would be exactly the same. As I say, there has been no change in government policy on this matter and so far as I am aware no change is contemplated. I cannot go any further than that.

The only
recommendation I can make of my speech is that it will not be the same because 1 have never spoken on this subject before. I sympathize greatly with the minister's problem and I am sorry that I do not remember the details of his speech last year. Assuming that the minister is aware, as I think he probably is, that there is a great
Supply-Finance
deal of distress among the people referred to by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, should he not make some statement? I know the minister cannot be Santa Claus to the whole world and if he tried to be I would be the first to criticize him. But if he could say something on this matter it would perhaps relieve the feelings of the people concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am sure that my hon. friend is as fully aware of the situation as I am. The civil service superannuation system of Canada is one of the most generous and favourable, if not the most favourable of any in the country. There are thousands and thousands of Canadians who have to provide their own social security and old age retirement fund by buying insurance, annuities and so on out of their own earnings and on a basis, if I may say so, somewhat less favourable than that enjoyed by civil servants. I have never felt that it was fair to the taxpayers of Canada as a whole that the civil servant who is entitled to benefits under this excellent and generous and fair superannuation plan should be on a preferred basis as compared with taxpayers generally.
